items.summary:

The Air Force Global Strike Command said the "routine test" late Tuesday at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, outside of Los Angeles, "was scheduled years ago and is not in response to world events."

"The ability to conduct these rigorous, realistic tests relies on the dedication of our Airmen and is foundational to ensuring the safety and surety of the Minuteman system," U.S. Air Force Gen. S.L. Davis, commander of Air Force Global Strike Command, said in a statement.

"Test opportunities, including this most recent launch, assess the entirety of the ICBM enterprise and provide various government agencies data to inform ICBM sustainment, engineering, and lifecycle analysis efforts," Air Force Global Strike Command added. "AFGSC has completed over 300 Minuteman III test launches to date."

I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech.

Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs.

Tariffs, agricultural purchases and rare earth minerals are all potential topics of conversation, and are in many ways intertwined, according to Ryan Yonk, an economic scholar and research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research who specializes in relations between the United States and China.

items.title: Alaska Dem Peltola defeats Sullivan, flipping 9th GOP Senate seat after 'decoy Dan' uproar
items.summary:
Democrats flipped a ninth GOP-held Senate seat in the 2026 midterm elections, with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeating two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in a state that President Donald Trump carried in 2024.

Peltola's victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the U.S. Senate.

"Alaskans have voted for change, and I'm so honored to be your next U.S. senator," Peltola said in a social media video released after The Associated Press called the race Tuesday two weeks after Election Day. "Together, we're gonna put an end to the era of self-serving politicians lining their own pockets at your expense. And together, we are going to put Alaska first."

Peltola defeated Sullivan with 50.1% of the vote, avoiding a ranked-choice vote count.

The contest emerged as one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races, with Republicans defending a seat in a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 13 percentage points in 2024, and Democrats eyeing a rare opportunity to make inroads in traditionally Republican territory.

The controversy deepened just days before Election Day when The New York Times reported that Peltola campaign aides, attorneys and national Democratic operatives had participated in a secret effort to recruit a candidate sharing the Republican incumbent's name.

According to the Times, text messages and interviews revealed a broader operation, internally dubbed the "ballot composition project,"…

items.title: POWs, teens among 6 US soldiers from Korean War identified seven decades later
items.summary:
At least six U.S. soldiers who went missing during the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been identified decades after their deaths.

The soldiers, who ranged in age from 18 to 28, all served in the U.S. Army, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) said. Five were junior enlisted soldiers or noncommissioned officers, including four corporals and one sergeant. The sixth was a commissioned officer, a first lieutenant.

Officials said the soldiers either died as prisoners of war or were presumed killed in action.

The soldiers identified were Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman, 18, of Illinois; 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert, 23, of Ohio; Cpl. Richard Neal Lennox, 18, of Michigan; Cpl. William Reynold Laughlin Jr., 21, of Oregon; Sgt. Joseph Alfred Platzkoester, 28, of Illinois; and Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, of Celina, Texas.

EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

Most of the soldiers had been buried for decades as "Unknowns" at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific, also known as the Punchbowl, in Honolulu, Hawaii. Their remains were later disinterred through DPAA initiatives…
items.t: POWs, teens among 6 US soldiers from Korean War identified seven decades later

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

  • Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero

In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.

That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work.

items.title: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial
items.summary:
Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing

At the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “welcome back” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “Breturn” has yet to catch on.

By Friday, the mood music will be louder still. A long-awaited reset summit is due to deliver the first fruits of Mr Burnham’s ongoing rapprochement with Brussels, in the form of new deals on food and drink, and emissions trading. items.title: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country

This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old.

There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service, careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation, scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold, the leisure centres closed, the mental health services for…

items.title: Even Hawaiʻi’s most Republican island can’t escape the blue wave
items.summary:
During the midterm elections, Ni‘ihau backed Democrats for their governors, casting 14 of their 21 votes for Josh Green and Derek Kawakami

The secluded island of Ni‘ihau has long been a Republican stronghold in deep blue Hawai‘i. Ni‘ihauans have an unusual tendency to unanimously support conservative candidates, like in 2020, when all 43 Ni‘ihauan voters cast their ballots for Donald Trump.

This has been the case since as far back as the early 1900s, when Ni‘ihau’s ballots were sometimes relayed to the neighboring island of Kaua‘i via carrier pigeon. The headline of one characteristic 1939 Honolulu Star Bulletin article reads – “Ni‘ihau Casts 59 Votes All For GOP as Usual.” Bush beat Kerry 39-0, Reagan beat Carter 56-1, and Nixon beat Kennedy 99-0.

items.title: Two reasons Democrats can overcome infighting next year | Robert Reich
items.summary:
The party’s big-tent approach has caused post-election feuding in the past. But a pair of singular goals can prevent it

Democrats usually suffer big tent disease. To win, they put together such large coalitions of voters – working class, middle class, Black people, Latinos, women, young people, moderates, liberals – that once they’re in office, intraparty feuds often threaten their agenda.

Will it happen again when they take power in January? I don’t think so. Two outside forces will keep Democrats glued together.
